items.q: Correct first aid position and pressure for epistaxis is what?
o: Sit leaning forward, pinch soft nose 10 to 15 minutes
items.exp: Forward lean prevents swallowing and airway soiling while soft part compression squeezes Kiesselbach plexus against septum. Bony bridge pressure compresses nothing useful; head back hides swallowed blood loss.
r: Incorrect. Lying back soils airway and bridge pinch misses vessels.
Correct. Forward lean, soft pinch, timed pressure.
Incorrect. Swallowed blood vomits and hides loss.
Incorrect. Blowing dislodges clot and worsens bleed.
items.kp: Forward, soft, fifteen: the first aid triad.

items.q: Why must silver nitrate cautery never be applied to both septal sides at same session?
o: Opposing cautery necroses cartilage causing perforation
items.exp: Septal cartilage feeds from overlying perichondrium on both sides; bilateral burns devascularise it producing perforation. Stage the sides weeks apart if both truly need treatment.
r: Incorrect. Staining is trivial skin effect.
Correct. Bilateral cautery perforates septum.
Incorrect. Smell area is superior, cautery is anterior inferior.
Incorrect. No pressor effect from local cautery.
items.kp: One side only: two burns make a hole.

items.q: Older hypertensive man bleeding down throat despite anterior pack most likely bleeds from where?
items.exp: Posterior bleeds from sphenopalatine branches in Woodruff area course down pharynx in older patients and escape anterior measures, needing posterior packing or SPA control and admission.
r: Incorrect. Anterior plexus bleeds out the nostril and cautery reaches it.
Correct. Posterior sphenopalatine source.
Incorrect. Skin bleeds externally visibly.
Incorrect. Front turbinate bleeds anteriorly.
items.kp: Down the throat in old age equals posterior source.

items.q: Posterior nasal packs require admission mainly due to which risks?
o: Hypoxia, airway and toxic shock complications
items.exp: Posterior packs can obstruct airway, trigger nasopulmonary reflex hypoxia (especially elderly, lung disease) and rarely toxic shock, so monitored admission with oxygen checks is standard.
r: Incorrect. Smell loss is not the admission driver.
Correct. Airway, hypoxia and toxic shock risks.
Incorrect. Perforation follows cautery or trauma more.
Incorrect. Ears unaffected by posterior packs.
items.kp: Back pack in place means bed and monitor.

items.q: Definitive endoscopic control for refractory posterior epistaxis targets which artery?
items.exp: Endoscopic SPA ligation or cautery at sphenopalatine foramen (crista ethmoidalis landmark) controls most refractory posterior bleeds with high success, largely replacing external carotid ligation.
r: Incorrect. Ethmoid control suits high anterior bleeds.
Correct. Ligate sphenopalatine artery endoscopically.
Incorrect. Neck ligation is historical backup.
Incorrect. Facial artery supplies lip and alar region.
items.kp: Tie the sphenopalatine and back bleeds stop.

items.q: Adolescent boy with recurrent unilateral epistaxis and nasal obstruction should be imaged for what before biopsy?
items.exp: Vascular angiofibroma in teenage males bleeds recurrently and must be imaged (CT/MRI with angiographic assessment) before any biopsy, which can haemorrhage catastrophically; resection follows embolisation planning.
r: Incorrect. Papilloma affects older adults.
Correct. Angiofibroma: image, never blind biopsy.
Incorrect. Polyps do not bleed this vascular pattern and biopsy still needs imaging first.
Incorrect. Spurs bleed mildly and are visible directly.
items.kp: Teen boy, blocked bleeding nose: image, do not biopsy.

items.q: Recurrent epistaxis with lip and tongue telangiectasia and family history suggests what?
items.exp: HHT (Osler Weber Rendu) gives mucocutaneous telangiectasia (lips, tongue, fingers), recurrent epistaxis and visceral arteriovenous malformations with autosomal dominant inheritance, needing systemic screening.
r: Incorrect. Von Willebrand lacks telangiectasia spots.
Correct. HHT telangiectasia pattern.
Incorrect. Scurvy gives gum and perifollicular bleeding.
Incorrect. Pressure aggravates but does not create spots.
items.kp: Spots on lips plus nosebleeds in family equals HHT.

items.q: Hypertension in acute epistaxis is best handled how?
o: Aggressive immediate lowering as primary cure
Control bleeding locally first; treat severe pressure per medical assessment
items.exp: Pressure often rises from pain and anxiety and rarely causes bleeds alone; local control comes first, then measured medical management of genuinely severe hypertension. Precipitate drops risk organ ischaemia.
r: Incorrect. Bleeding control is local, not pressure crash.
Correct. Local control first, judged pressure care after.
Incorrect. Severe sustained hypertension still needs care.
Incorrect. Sedation is selective, not routine.
items.kp: Stop the nose first, then judge the pressure.

items.q: After successful cautery, which advice prevents early rebleeding?
o: Avoid blowing, straining and hot showers; use humidification
items.exp: Protecting the eschar (no blowing, sneezing open mouthed, avoiding heat and straining, saline or ointment humidification) for about a week prevents clot disruption rebleeds.
r: Incorrect. Blowing shears the fresh eschar.
Correct. Protect clot and humidify.
Incorrect. Hydration helps mucosa; restriction harms.
Incorrect. Picking restarts anterior bleeds.
items.kp: Leave the scab alone and keep it moist.

items.q: Embolisation for epistaxis is reserved selectively because of which feared complications?
o: Stroke and ophthalmic blindness via collateral vessels
items.exp: External carotid branches anastomose with ophthalmic and cerebral circulations, so embolic stroke and blindness are rare but defining risks, reserving embolisation for surgical failures or unfit patients.
r: Incorrect. Perforation is cautery complication.
Correct. Stroke and blindness from collaterals.
Incorrect. Smell risk is minor by comparison.
Incorrect. Infection relates to packing duration.
items.kp: Emboli can reach eye and brain: reserve it.
